title: How Police Chases Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss police chases: the lack of laws restricting pursuits, deaths and injuries to bystanders, police driver training (including the Colorado State Patrol Emergency Vehicles Operation course), pursuit vehicle modifications (Crown Victoria police package, fire suppression, heavy-duty components, vinyl rear seats), light bars, pursuit-stopping tools like spike strips, roadblocks and the LAIR/HALT laser system, helicopter coverage, pursuit policies (Washington D.C., Des Moines, Orange County Florida), the pit maneuver, cop reality TV shows, sovereign immunity and liability. Also includes a call-out asking listeners for iTunes reviews and Kiva support, and an ad for Audible.
topics: Colorado State Patrol Emergency Vehicles Operation course

segments.title: Opening banter and police chase introduction
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, introduce the law enforcement series topic of police chases, and Chuck shares a story of fleeing police in Athens as a passenger.

segments.title: Chase deaths and lack of pursuit laws
segments.summary: Discussion that there are almost no laws restricting police chases, activists calling for restrictions, and statistics that about 140 bystanders were killed in a year and roughly one person a day dies in chases. Atlanta cases are mentioned.

segments.title: Police driver training
segments.summary: Police academy driving training is brief, with about two days on high-speed pursuit, and older departments offered none. Ed Gorbanowski is cited on driving skills, and the Colorado State Patrol emergency vehicles course is described with low-friction skid pads and realistic street scenarios.

segments.title: Pursuit vehicles and modifications
segments.summary: The Ford Crown Victoria is the most common police car, though departments are moving to other models. Discussion of the Crown Vic fuel-fire suppression system versus the Pinto's fire problem, and police-package upgrades such as more horsepower, reinforced seats, extra coolers, heavier alternators, and vinyl rear seats.

segments.title: Light bars and sirens
segments.summary: Police light bars debuted in the 1970s after lights on fenders proved less visible. Colors of emergency lights discussed, and sirens in movies like Dirty Harry.

segments.title: Stopping chases: spikes, roadblocks, laser and microwave tech
segments.summary: Methods to end chases include spike strips, roadblocks with caution about funneling suspects into neighborhoods, and modern tools such as microwave electrical disabling and a laser fuel-cutoff system that requires a vehicle microchip.

segments.title: Pursuit decisions, supervisors, and the pit maneuver
segments.summary: Officers run plates to decide whether to pursue; violent offenses justify chases while traffic violations do not, and about 91.4 percent of chases were for non-violent crimes. Supervisors monitor and can call off pursuits; helicopters can follow from above. The pit maneuver is explained as a turn-based technique requiring clearance.

segments.title: Chase TV coverage, legal liability, and wrap-up
segments.summary: Reality shows like Cops are criticized for one-sided coverage. The O.J. Simpson chase is recalled. Legal points: no laws restrict pursuits, Washington D.C., Des Moines, and Orange County, Florida policies are compared, and sovereign immunity and suits against departments in California and Atlanta are discussed. Hosts close with a call for iTunes reviews, Kiva support, and an Audible ad.
